From a question I asked on Zhihu: What books and textbooks do acousticians use?

The original question:

Here is the situation. On the one hand, acoustics is a niche field, but because it is so interdisciplinary there are foreign-language books for almost every corner of it. On the other, there are only a handful of acoustics books in Chinese, translations included. And books in one’s own language are key to promoting and popularizing a discipline.

So I have long wanted to translate an outstanding foreign acoustics book, and some friends on Zhihu have encouraged me. I’d like to ask my fellow acousticians:

1. Which area of acoustics do you work in?

2. Could you share your book list, with a short description of each book?

3. Which book would you recommend? Tell us about its main focus, intended readers, structure, level of difficulty, prerequisites and so on.

Download links would be much appreciated, to make sharing easier.

Below, the section on foreign-language books is my own answer. The section on Chinese books is the answer by Tone Liu, a leading voice on acoustics on Zhihu and the only Outstanding Answerer in its acoustics topic. The “Read more” link of the original post leads to the Zhihu question itself, where many other colleagues have left excellent answers. Do take a look.

From Ziyu on Zhihu

1. Which area of acoustics do you work in?

My PhD was on modeling moving sound sources for auralization, which mainly involved microphone arrays, beamforming and sound synthesis. I also worked a little on 3D reproduction in virtual acoustics: binaural hearing, HRTFs, crosstalk cancellation (CTC) and so on.

Today I mainly develop noise measurement products, and I deal with a wide range of industries: automotive OEMs and suppliers at every tier, aerospace, building and environmental acoustics, end-of-line (EOL) quality control on production lines, white goods and more. On the technical side, it’s hard to name any one specialty. I’m in “brick of the revolution” mode, as the old Chinese slogan has it: put me wherever I’m needed.

2. Could you share your book list, with a short description of each book?

First, here are all the acoustics books I have saved: 64 of them, though that certainly doesn’t cover everything.

The main ones I have read:

Fundamentals of acoustics:

Kuttruff: Acoustics

An introductory text, fairly easy to follow.

Vorländer: Auralization

Not very detailed on acoustic theory, but the authoritative book on auralization.

Jacobsen: Fundamentals of general linear acoustics

Covers the fundamentals with experiments and examples; concrete, intuitive and easy to understand.

Morse: Theoretical acoustics

The most mathematically complete acoustics book there is. Lots of formulas, fairly heavy going, and it demands a solid mathematical background.

On microphone arrays and beamforming:

Johnson: Array signal processing
van Trees: Optimum Array Processing

Johnson’s is the more approachable; the other is full of mathematics and a bit hard to digest. I have also read a little of the book by Professor Bai in Taiwan, but not enough to comment.

Psychoacoustics:

Zwicker: Psychoacoustics

The bible of psychoacoustics. Fairly easy to understand, with a wealth of experimental data.

I haven’t read any of these cover to cover, and there’s no need to. I look things up when I need them. When several books cover the same ground, I focus on the one most to my taste and read the others alongside it for comparison. Different authors look at problems from different angles, and you learn a great deal that way.

3. Which book would you recommend? Tell us about its main focus, intended readers, structure, level of difficulty, prerequisites and so on.

Fundamentals of General Linear Acoustics by Finn Jacobsen

I have recommended this book in several of my answers.

In the preface, the author introduces the book roughly as follows.

First, it links acoustic theory with industrial practice. The acoustics group at DTU (the Technical University of Denmark) collaborates with many companies, and Professor Jacobsen himself combined extensive experience of real industrial projects with many contributions to theory. So the book builds on the theoretical foundations of acoustics but leans toward practical application.

Second, it takes the interdisciplinary nature of acoustics into account. To make it accessible to readers from many backgrounds, it largely does without mechanical and electrical analogies and explains the mathematics purely from a physical point of view.

Finally, the author modestly describes the book as paving the way for more complete “big books,” such as Theoretical Acoustics (Morse) and Acoustics: An Introduction to Its Physical Principles and Applications (Pierce).

The book is quite accessible. The author says he wrote it for readers at master’s level and above, but undergraduates will have no trouble with it. Anyone with a reasonable grounding in university physics and mathematics will find it manageable.

It has nine chapters:

  1. Introduction

  2. Fundamentals of acoustic wave motion

  3. Simple sound fields

  4. Basic acoustic measurements

  5. The concept of impedance

  6. Sound energy, sound power, sound intensity and sound absorption

  7. Duct acoustics

  8. Sound in enclosures

  9. Sound radiation and scattering

And four appendices:

A. Complex representation of harmonic functions of time

B. Signal analysis and processing

C. Cylindrical and spherical Bessel functions

D. Fundamentals of probability and random variables

Because the book takes real industrial work as its starting point, the appendices cover the signal processing most relevant to acoustics, and that orientation shows in the individual chapters too.

Chapter 9, for example, really belongs earlier in the book, but it ties in with practical applications that draw on everything before it, so it comes last. After the fundamentals, each section is followed by the techniques that build on it, such as beamforming, near-field acoustic holography (NAH) and Ambisonics.

Chapter 4 is devoted entirely to acoustic measurement, and every chapter also covers the relevant measurements and applications.

Or take Section 6.5, which spends several pages explaining what sound intensity is used for. At university I often had the nagging feeling: what are all these formulas actually for? What use are they? And I usually forgot them soon after the exam. Our Chinese textbooks tend to present conclusions, nothing but the “dry goods,” a style said to have been borrowed from the Soviet Union. European and American textbooks do the opposite: they care about the story and lay out the background and context before explaining a principle. This book puts particular weight on applications. Right after explaining a principle, it tells you where you can use what you have just learned, so the knowledge sticks.

Another strength is its many examples. In the chapter on impedance, for instance, it gives three examples when it introduces mechanical impedance, which makes the idea easier to grasp and more memorable.

All in all, at around 300 pages, the book is on the slim side. Its explanations of the theory are clear, so it is very friendly to beginners; it doesn’t scare readers off by opening with a wall of equations. For professionals who have been in the field for a while, it is also a good reference for refreshing the fundamentals. As the author says, it is the right book to read before tackling the more comprehensive “big books.”

From Tone Liu on Zhihu:

My research is in physical acoustics and artificial acoustic structures (what are usually called metamaterials, a term with three competing translations in Chinese). I also follow work in fields such as acoustic testing and audio.

I’m embarrassed to admit that in recent years I have had fewer and fewer chances to read textbooks systematically; most of the time I go straight to reviews and papers. The heavyweights here have covered plenty of English books, so let me add a few in Chinese:

1. Fundamentals of Acoustics by Gonghuan Du, Zhemin Zhu and Xiufen Gong, Nanjing University Press

Probably the most widely read introductory acoustics book in Chinese. It is very systematic and easy to follow. It goes from the vibration of a point mass to the vibration of continuous elastic bodies, and on to the propagation, radiation, reception and dissipation of airborne sound, covering the physical basis of most acoustic problems. It also has separate sections on sound fields in rooms, nonlinear acoustics and elastic waves in solids. Simple practical applications and everyday physical phenomena are woven throughout, which helps understanding.

2. Theoretical Acoustics by Hailan Zhang, Higher Education Press

A textbook from the Graduate School of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Its overall framework resembles Fundamentals of Acoustics, but the mathematical methods and theory go deeper. Professor Zhang works mainly on acoustic testing, including medical ultrasound, non-destructive testing and geophysical exploration, so the book pays particular attention to transient problems, and its treatment of elastic waves is more thorough.

3. Fundamentals of Modern Acoustical Theory by Dah-You Maa, Science Press

I haven’t read it all the way through. Here Professor Maa moves the material on vibration, which usually comes first, into an appendix and concentrates on acoustic (airborne sound) problems themselves. Compared with the two books above, it adds aeroacoustics, thermoacoustics and active noise control, and leans more toward noise and vibration control, which was Professor Maa’s main field.

4. Principles of Acoustics by Jianchun Cheng, Science Press

I bought it but haven’t read it carefully yet… Professor Cheng’s command of theory is formidable, and he clearly poured a great deal of effort into this book. Its style leans toward physics, and it goes deeper and wider than Fundamentals of Acoustics. Since I haven’t read it carefully, I’ll leave it at that.

5. Acoustic Measurements by Ke’an Chen, Xiangyang Zeng and Haiying Li, Science Press

A fairly systematic introduction to the principles and methods of acoustic measurement for noise, building acoustics, environmental acoustics and more.

6. Handbook of Acoustics by Dah-You Maa and Hao Shen, Science Press

A hefty tome. An encyclopedic reference that covers more or less every field of acoustics.

7. Ultrasonic Waves in Solid Media by Joseph L. Rose, translated into Chinese by Cunfu He, Science Press

A book on elastic waves, from bulk waves to surface and interface waves and on to guided waves in all kinds of structures.

As for my own field, acoustic metamaterials, there are no really good monographs yet. What does exist is mostly a patchwork of review-style chapters, each written by a different big name. That’s probably mainly because the field is still young (less than 20 years old) and its boundaries keep expanding. The field has always been controversial; some people in traditional acoustics in particular see it as hype or as unusable in practice. Still, it seems more and more people are joining in, and quite a few are genuinely pushing toward engineering applications. Personally, I think metamaterials have at least breathed some life into acoustics, a discipline that is showing its age. It really does feel as if acoustics has little left but engineering problems, with no fundamental frontier questions (or only fundamental questions too hard to make progress on, such as nonlinearity).

Let me recommend a few reviews:

[1] Cummer, S. A., Christensen, J., & Alù, A. (2016). Controlling sound with acoustic metamaterials. Nature Reviews Materials, 1(3), 16001.

[2] Ma, G., & Sheng, P. (2016). Acoustic metamaterials: From local resonances to broad horizons. Science Advances, 2(2), e1501595.

[3] Assouar, B., Liang, B., Wu, Y., Li, Y., Cheng, J. C., & Jing, Y. (2018). Acoustic metasurfaces. Nature Reviews Materials, 1.
